slides.title: Chapter 7: Scripts and Signatures
slides.sub: Authorization and authentication: scripts that lock coins, signatures that unlock them

items.body: Figure: locking and unlocking scripts, Antonopoulos and Harding, Mastering Bitcoin 3e, CC BY-SA 4.0. Python 3.14.6, no Bitcoin Core node.

slides.notes: This deck explains how Bitcoin decides who may spend an output. The output carries a lock, the spender supplies the key, and every node runs both and accepts only a true result. Every spend shown ran in the chapter's own interpreter; no Bitcoin Core node was available where it was built.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.sub: Nine parts; every number is a slide you can jump to

items.label: 3. Locking a coin to a key
code examples with a picture of each result

slides.notes: The route has nine parts that follow the order in which Bitcoin gained its spending conditions. Three true stories and fifteen code examples are spread across them. The examples are listed in the same order in the chapter code tab of the course page, so every slide can be rerun.
slides.take: Nine parts, fifteen runs and three true stories

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.sub: Its own competency questions; we return to each

items: How do an output script and an input script together decide a spend?
Why is Script not Turing complete, and why can every node verify it?
How do key hashes, multisignatures and script hashes move cost to the spender?
How do lock time and sequence make a spend wait?
How does segregated witness fix malleability without splitting the network?
What does taproot hide, and what does a key path or script path reveal?
What does tapscript change in the language?

slides.notes: The seven questions are the chapter's own, shortened so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all seven has understood the chapter.

slides.title: Scripts and the Script language
slides.sub: A script is a lock and key recipe that every node checks the same way.

slides.title: Script is arithmetic on a stack
slides.sub: The smallest script of the chapter, run in the chapter's interpreter

groups.note: A script is read left to right; numbers are pushed and operations use the top items.
Change the five to a six and the same script fails.
The assembler turns the five words into five bytes.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - names as in the chapter setup

items.body: Result: the same script with a five and a six
The sum is five, so the first script ends true and the second false. The five words assemble to five bytes.

slides.notes: Script reads its words from left to right. Numbers are pushed on the stack, and OP_ADD replaces the top two by their sum. OP_EQUAL compares the sum with five, so the spend is true with five and false with six. It is example 1 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Numbers are pushed; an operation takes its inputs from the top

slides.title: The OP_RETURN bug of 2010
slides.sub: Joined scripts against separate scripts

groups.note: The first software joined both scripts into one program that stopped at OP_RETURN.
Today the scripts run apart, and OP_RETURN makes the spend fail.
Only the real secret opens the lock, in both engines.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, K and the chapter setup as on slide 7

items.body: Result: a spend that has no secret, and one that has
In the old engine OK means that anyone could spend the coin. Today the same input fails with OP_RETURN.

slides.notes: In 2010 the software joined the input script and the output script into one program. An input script of 1 then OP_RETURN ended the run with a true value before the lock ran. Today the scripts run apart. It is example 2 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Run the two scripts apart, and fail closed on anything unknown

slides.title: The script that ended with a true result
slides.sub: A bug of 2010 that let anyone spend any output

items.cap: Bust of Satoshi Nakamoto, Budapest - Fekist, CC BY-SA 4.0

items: WHAT: On 28 July 2010 two bugs were shown on the test network; one let a stranger spend coins that were not theirs.
WHY: The first software joined input and output script into one program, and OP_RETURN jumped to its end with a true result.
HOW: An input script of 1 then OP_RETURN ended the run true; version 0.3.5 fixed it, and later versions run the scripts apart.
SO WHAT: Many unused opcodes were disabled; in tapscript such values, like OP_LSHIFT (152), are now OP_SUCCESS.

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2010-07-28. On 28 July 2010 two bugs were discovered and demonstrated on the test network. The lesson: run the two scripts separately, and fail closed on anything unknown.

slides.title: A DER signature, strict and loose
slides.sub: Why the encoding of a signature is a consensus rule

groups.note: A signature is made over the hash of a message.
With its hash type it is 72 bytes, starts with 0x30 and has a low s.
A padded signature passes old rules but fails the strict DER rule.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, K and the chapter setup as on slide 7

items.body: Result: one signature, two rule sets
The same padded signature passes without the DER rule and fails with it, with the error SIG_DER.

slides.notes: A signature is two numbers, r and s, written in DER with a hash type at the end. A padded form was once accepted. Since BIP66 only the strict form is valid, which is the rule behind the fork of 2015. It is example 4 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A rule that nodes check for themselves cannot be skipped

slides.title: Half the miners did not check the block
slides.sub: Strict DER signatures, and the fork of 4 July 2015

items.cap: A bitcoin mining farm, 2014 - Marko Ahtisaari, CC BY 2.0

items: WHAT: On 4 July 2015, at block 363,725, strict DER signatures (BIP66) took effect, and a fork of six blocks followed.
WHY: About half of the hash rate mined without fully validating, so it built on an invalid block of a miner that had not upgraded.
HOW: The fork lasted from 02:10 to 03:50 UTC, a second of three blocks followed on 5 July, and the first showed no double spend.
SO WHAT: Bitcoin Core 0.9.5 and later checked the rule and were unaffected: a rule you do not check protects nobody.

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2015-07-04. BIP66 made strict DER the only valid encoding of a signature, and it took effect once 950 of the last 1,000 blocks were version 3, which happened early on 4 July 2015, at block 363,725. The lesson: a rule that you do not check for yourself protects nobody.

slides.sub: A multisignature is a vault that opens when enough directors turn their keys.

slides.title: A 2-of-3 multisignature
slides.sub: Signatures in key order, and the extra element

groups.note: Signatures must follow the order of the keys; one signature is too few.
CHECKMULTISIG pops one item too many; a non-empty dummy is refused.
The script itself is 105 bytes, mostly three public keys.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, K and the chapter setup as on slide 7

items.body: Result: five trials of a 2-of-3 lock
The script is 105 bytes long. Only signatures in the order of the keys, behind an empty dummy, pass.

slides.notes: A two-of-three lock lists three keys and wants two signatures in the same order. A single signature fails. The opcode also pops one item too many, so a dummy sits in front and must be empty. It is example 5 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The signatures must follow the order of the keys, after one empty dummy

slides.title: Pay to script hash
slides.sub: A script hash is a sealed envelope that shows only a code number.

items.meaning: The lock holds only the hash; the script is revealed at spending.
items.analogy: Think of sealing a contract in an envelope.

slides.notes: A long lock is costly for the payer. Pay to script hash puts only a hash in the output and lets the spender reveal the script. We build one and watch a wrong script fail.

slides.title: Pay to script hash
slides.sub: The payer sees a hash, the spender shows the script

The spender reveals the script; a script that does not hash to the lock fails.
Addresses of this kind start with a 3.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, K and the chapter setup as on slide 7

items.body: Result: the hash lock and two reveals
The lock is 23 bytes however long the script is. A script that does not match the hash fails.

slides.notes: The output holds only the 20-byte hash of the script, so the payer pays for a short lock. The spender reveals the script, nodes hash it, compare, and then run it. A script that hashes differently fails. It is example 6 in the chapter code tab of the course page.

slides.title: Data and timelocks
slides.sub: A timelock is a post-dated cheque; a data output is a note on a noticeboard.

items.meaning: A few bytes of data go on chain without a spendable coin.
items.analogy: Think of a noticeboard that nobody can walk away with.

items.meaning: A transaction or a coin that waits for a fixed time or height.
items.analogy: Think of a savings bond with a fixed date.

items.meaning: A coin that waits for an age, counted from the day it was mined.
items.analogy: Think of a gift card that works a week after purchase.

slides.notes: Two special locks. One records a few bytes of data and can never be spent. The others make a coin wait, until a time or block, or for an age counted from the day it was mined.

slides.title: Data and timelocks: concepts (1 of 3)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Data Recording Output (OP_RETURN)
items.meaning: An unspendable output that carries a few bytes of data.
items.analogy: Think of a note pinned to a public noticeboard.

items.label: Transaction Lock Time Limitations
items.meaning: Lock time stops a transaction, not a spender.
items.analogy: Think of a post-dated cheque that its writer can replace before the date.

items.label: Check Lock Time Verify (OP_CLTV)
items.meaning: A script rule: this coin is not spendable before a time or height.
items.analogy: Think of a savings bond that cannot be cashed before its date.

items.label: Relative Timelocks
items.meaning: A wait counted from the day the coin was mined.
items.analogy: Think of a gift card that works only a week after purchase.

slides.title: Hard fork or soft fork?
slides.sub: Why segregated witness could be activated without splitting the network

left.head: A hard fork loosens the rules
rows: Blocks that old nodes reject become valid.
Every node must upgrade, or the chain splits.
Like a new road standard that old cars cannot use.

right.head: A soft fork tightens the rules
rows: New nodes reject more; they accept nothing new.
Old nodes still follow the chain and accept its blocks.
Like a stricter speed limit that old cars can still obey.

slides.notes: Segregated witness was a soft fork. Old nodes saw the new outputs as anyone-can-spend scripts and accepted the blocks, while upgraded nodes enforced the witness rules. That is why it could be activated without a split.
slides.take: A soft fork can only restrict; old nodes keep accepting the blocks

slides.title: From a patented signature to taproot
slides.sub: Taproot took effect at block 709,632 in 2021

items.cap: Claus-Peter Schnorr, 1986 - Konrad Jacobs, CC BY-SA 2.0 de

items: WHAT: At block 709,632, mined on 14 November 2021, the taproot rules and Schnorr signatures (BIPs 340 to 342) took effect.
WHY: Claus Schnorr had patented his signature, which kept it out of open standards for almost two decades; ECDSA was used instead.
HOW: BIP340 was assigned in January 2020; a soft fork then added taproot and tapscript to the running chain.
SO WHAT: A key path spend is one 64-byte signature that looks the same whether one person or a million made it.

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2021-11-14. Claus Schnorr patented the signature algorithm he discovered and kept it out of open standards and open-source software for almost two decades, so cryptographers of the early 1990s built the DSA family that led to the ECDSA signatures Bitcoin used from its first release.

slides.title: Opcodes kept for upgrades
slides.sub: OP_SUCCESS in tapscript

rows: n = sum(1 for o in range(256) if L.is_op_success(o))
groups.note: In tapscript, 87 opcode values succeed on sight.

The same word, a disabled shift, fails in an old script.

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.sub: One line per group of parts, each provable from its slides

items: A coin is locked by a script; the spender's script is the key, and the two run apart on a stack.
Key hashes, multisignatures and script hashes lock a coin to what the spender can prove, and move the long lock to the spender.
Lock time and sequence make a spend wait, and flow control gives one output several ways out.
Segregated witness moves the proof out of the identifier, as a soft fork that old nodes accept.
Taproot commits to a tree of scripts with one key, so agreement looks like a single signature.

slides.notes: These five lines are the deck in miniature. A line that feels unproven should send you back to its code slide, because every result in it was computed there. The chapter code tab of the course page lets you rerun all fifteen examples.
slides.take: If a line feels unproven, the code slide of its part carries the receipt
